excludedAssessments.summary: The elementary multiletter analysis is largely correct: independent concatenation makes M_n superadditive; 0 <= M_n <= 2n; Fekete's lemma gives the normalized limit/supremum; an exact witness S_n improves the one-letter benchmark exactly when S_n > nL_RTD and propagates to kS_n; and fixed-n equality is not a capacity converse. However, the capacity lower bound requires the applicable private-message Marton coding theorem, and identifying L_RTD with the full one-letter optimum M_1(P) requires a separate binary-input Marton evaluation. Neither necessary theorem is proved or supplied as admissible declared-reference evidence. There is also an unresolved finite-auxiliary scope issue if M_n permits arbitrary auxiliary spaces. Finally, the computation reported for the 33-decimal prefix lacks interval or rounding-error certification, although the warning not to treat a prefix as an exact upper bound is correct. Thus the bounded record does not establish the full claim.
scopeQualifications: The witness 'if and only if' concerns whether that witness's directly normalized value S_n/n exceeds L_RTD; failure of a numerical certificate does not show that the law's exact objective cannot exceed the threshold.
Super-symbol normalization is correct conditional on an applicable Marton theorem for the exact private-message and average-error conventions.
The definition of M_n must either restrict U,V,W to finite alphabets or be supplemented by a finite-approximation/cardinality argument.
The stated decimal is only computationally reproduced, not rigorously enclosed.
Equality M_n=nL_RTD at a fixed n supplies neither a capacity upper bound nor exclusion of improvements at other blocklengths or by other coding schemes.
evidenceIssues: No declared reference establishes Marton's applicable private-message coding theorem.
No declared reference establishes M_1(P)=L_RTD for the governed binary-input channel.
Finite-auxiliary sufficiency is not established if arbitrary auxiliary spaces are admitted by the displayed definition.
The high-precision decimal calculation uses no certified interval arithmetic or proved rounding-error bound.
